entry.trigger_summary: The mechanical system he and William Eckhardt taught the Turtles entered on Donchian channel breakouts: System 1 on 20-day highs/lows, System 2 on 55-day highs/lows. His own earlier pit trading was more discretionary but followed the same trend-with-breakout logic (hence discretion = hybrid).
entry.notes: System 1 also had a rule outside this taxonomy: skip the 20-day breakout if the previous breakout signal would have been a winner (take the 55-day failsafe instead). Position limits capped units in closely correlated markets.

exit.notes: Initial stop at 2N (twice the 20-day ATR-like N) from entry; the effective trailing exit was an opposite Donchian breakout (10-day for System 1, 20-day for System 2), exiting the entire position at once.

risk_per_trade_pct.note: Derivation: the published rules size one unit so that a 1N price move equals about 1% of account equity, and the initial stop is 2N from entry, so one unit risks about 2% of equity. max_drawdown_rule.note: Turtle rules: for each 10% drawdown, trade as if the account were 20% smaller, restoring size as equity recovers.

portfolio_heat_cap.note: Turtle position limits: max 4 units per market, 6 units in closely correlated markets, 12 units total in one direction. Pyramiding added units at 0.5N intervals up to the 4-unit market cap.

risk.notes: All numeric risk rules here are from the published system he taught the Turtles; Dennis never publicly disclosed equivalent parameters for his own earlier discretionary trading.

sizing.notes: N-based (ATR-style) unit sizing so each unit represented roughly equal volatility exposure across markets (Original Turtle Rules).

entry.trigger_summary: Two published mechanical systems. (1) The weekly/4-week rule (the original Donchian channel): buy and cover shorts when price exceeds the highs of the prior four full calendar weeks; sell and go short on a new 4-week low — an always-in-the-market reversal system. (2) The 5- and 20-day moving average method (developed at Hayden Stone, 1960): trade in the direction of a 20-day MA crossing, but only after price penetrates the MA by a preset number of price-scaled units (e.g., larger absolute penetration required for higher-priced commodities) with day-sequencing confirmation rules; the 5-day MA governs shorter-term liquidation.
entry.notes: His general guides tell traders to treat volume expansion after a quiet period as significant, and his supplemental 5/20 rules require minimum penetration before acting — paraphrased from sources 2-3. The 4-week rule itself has no confirmation conditions.

exit.notes: In the 4-week system the exit is the opposite channel signal (position reverses at a new 4-week extreme against you). In the 5/20 method, longs are liquidated when price closes back below the 5-day MA (with confirmation), shorts vice versa. His guidelines separately advise 'judicious' use of stop orders placed with reference to chart formations to cap losses and protect profits — hence structure/chart-based initial stop basis (sources 2-3).

risk.notes: He published qualitative risk guidance (limit losses, protect profits with stops, trade light when direction is unclear) but no numeric per-trade risk, drawdown or heat rules — all fields honestly null (source 2).

sizing.notes: Mapped from his published general guides: carry light commitments when market direction is uncertain and heavier positions when a sustained move is anticipated (he also noted long-side advances tend to yield larger percentage gains than equal declines). Qualitative rule, no numbers (source 2).

psychology_rules.paraphrase: His overriding published guideline — "limit losses and ride profits, irrespective of all other rules" (Donchian, trading guidelines) — put loss-cutting above every other consideration.
The companion half of the same overriding guide: stay with a clearly defined sustained move and let the trend produce the profit rather than taking it early.
Act only on clearly defined moves and stand aside in sideways ranges; he warned that trading indistinct conditions produces whipsaw losses, and against hasty decisions driven by popular opinion.
